title: Lhabab Duchen again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kathina, and Visakha noticing monks standing in the rain. Your line was the rains end in gifts. What useful thing did you give, and to whom? Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

What do you owe the person who gave birth to you? People have tried to answer that with flowers, phone calls, money, or a seat at the head of the table. The Buddha's own story has a strange shape here. Tradition says his mother, Maya, died soon after his birth, so he never had the chance to repay her in the ordinary ways. After his awakening, the story goes, he went up to the heaven where she had been reborn, and spent a rains retreat teaching her. Then he came down. In Tibet, the day of that descent is Lhabab Duchen. You've met the staircase of the gods before. Today, ask why he went up at all.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU OWE YOUR MOTHER?` → `HE NEVER KNEW HER.` → `WHY DID HE GO UP?`

segments.voice: First, a debt that can't be paid. In the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha says there are two people you can never fully repay: your mother and your father. Even if you carried one on each shoulder for a whole long life, washed and fed them, and made them rulers of the earth, it still wouldn't be enough. They brought you up, fed you, and showed you this world. Second, the one way it can be repaid. The same discourse turns. If your parents lack faith, you help them toward faith. If they lack virtue, toward virtue. If they're stingy, toward generosity. If they lack wisdom, toward wisdom. That, it says, repays them. Third, the story in that light. Read Lhabab Duchen beside that discourse, and the descent from heaven looks like a son repaying a debt. He didn't bring his mother gold. He brought her the best thing he had, the teaching. Fourth, the coming down. When the season ended, he didn't stay up there. Tradition says he descended at Sankassa, to crowds waiting below. In Tibet, Lhabab Duchen is kept with offerings, circling holy places, and giving. Elsewhere, at the end of the rains, the same descent is remembered with alms rounds. He went up to honor one person and came back down for everyone. Some readers see in that the whole shape of the path: go deep for someone you love, then return to the ordinary crowd.
screen: `A DEBT YOU CAN'T REPAY.` · `UNLESS YOU HELP THEM GROW.` · `HE BROUGHT HER THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `HE CAME DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Let your mother come to mind, or whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a father who did both jobs, a foster parent, a teacher. If that relationship is painful, you can choose someone else who cared for you, or simply rest with the breath. Picture their hands. Something they made, carried, or fixed for you. Breathe in, and remember one specific thing they gave. Breathe out, and let a little thanks go toward them, living or gone. Stay with that until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Lhabab Duchen. The Tibetan holy day of the Buddha's descent from heaven, after teaching his mother. Today's word.
Your line: he came down. Today, honor your mother, or whoever mothered you, in one concrete way: a call, a visit, a photo set out, a kind word said aloud. Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

howItsDone: On Lhabab Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, make offerings, recite prayers and mantras, circle stupas and holy places, and give generously; in Theravada lands the descent is remembered with alms rounds at the end of the rains.

myth: the discourse says you can repay parents by carrying them on your shoulders
even that isn't enough. helping them toward faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom repays them.
in tradition, the Buddha taught his mother in a heaven, then came back down
he spent a rains retreat there, then descended to the crowds.
Lhabab Duchen remembers the Buddha's birth
it remembers his descent from heaven after teaching his mother.

fork.setup: you want to repay your parents for everything. the discourse in today's lesson gives one way. what is it?
options: help them toward faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
carry them on your shoulders for life.
fork.reveal: wealth and carrying aren't enough, the discourse says. helping them grow in those four ways repays them.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit mata: mother. Maya, the Buddha's mother, is at the center of this day's story.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lhabab Duchen is about a miracle staircase.
what it means: a son going up to give his mother the best thing he had, then coming back down for everyone.
what a scholar hears: the Numbered Discourses on the unrepayable debt to parents, read beside the descent at Sankassa.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary (the twin miracle and the descent at Sankassa)

notes: AN 2.33 (numbering varies, AN 2.31–32 in some editions) paraphrased: one parent on each shoulder for a hundred years ('a whole long life' in the voice), anointing, bathing, ruling the earth, still not repaid; establishing them in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom repays them. Confirm the sutta number and the paraphrase.
'His mother, Maya, died soon after his birth': tradition gives seven days; the number is left out per the claims rule.
Descent at Sankassa and the rains retreat in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three come from the commentarial tradition; framed as 'tradition says'.
Theravada end-of-rains alms rounds (Tak Bat Devo) described generally; confirm.
Practice offers alternatives for listeners whose mothers are absent or whose relationship is painful.
Editor: Maya's early death is not in AN 2.33; framed it as "tradition says" and varied the next sentence to avoid two "tradition says" in a row.
